role.altitude: The cashier's week is still the till: prices, questions, the phone and calls for help. Less of it is re-keying a known price, hunting a binder, or announcing a page the whole shop can hear. Overrides, policy exceptions and stopping a sale stay with the cashier's judgement and the duty supervisor.
reach: Counter and rental clerks: which prices and procedures the till will accept before a colleague checks a reservation
Parts salespersons: a reason code plus an item id, instead of a voice page to the storeroom
skills_to_grow: Tell a price-file gap from a customer holding the wrong item
Read a quoted policy sentence and refuse to say more than it says
Pick a page reason that tells the colleague what to bring
role.ambitious_version: A shopper with a standard basket sees the price the till will charge, hears a short procedure the cashier has checked against the quoted sentence, and a colleague is already on the way because the page named the item. The cashier stays on the awkward sale, the exception and the person who needs them.

tasks.short: Identify the price of goods or admission and total the bill.

steps.what: Scan barcodes or admission codes so the till prices each line.
Key the price from a shelf label when the scan fails.
Write a price override request when the charged price is disputed.
Approve or refuse the price override against the shelf price.
Read the tabulated bill total and discounts to the customer.

tasks.design: The item price, tax class and promotion id live in the {ERP} and are the only prices the {OTHER} point-of-sale till may charge for goods. Admission and service codes are till PLUs owned by the store manager. Standard barcodes can be scanned by the customer where the store already runs that lane; the cashier keys a failed scan and writes a price override request. The duty supervisor approves that exact request before the till posts it, and the customer-facing total replaces adding the bill up again.
tasks.previous_blocker: The till already stored barcodes, but a missing scan, a local promotion or a paper price list still sent the cashier to the shelf and a supervisor across the floor. There was no single request snapshot to approve.
tasks.enabler_now: Item search and a manager-approval prompt are settings on the till. Self-scan is already common in equipped grocery stores, and the loss rate is known, so a person stays on exceptions rather than a new kind of system.
tasks.still_hard: Unmarked goods, admission exceptions and a disputed price still need a person. Missed scans on self-scan are a few percent of transactions and raise shrink, so the cashier's check does not disappear.
tasks.human_edge: The cashier sees a switched label or a customer who cannot use the scanner. The duty supervisor decides a price that is not on the file. Neither is a lookup.

ambition.what: Every disputed price is checked against the shelf price on the same request snapshot, including on a short-staffed evening.

tasks.altitude: Less of the shift is re-keying a known price. The cashier still runs assisted tills and awkward or age-restricted items, and can stop a line that looks wrong. They do not gain the right to override a price.

reach.task: Quote an admission or hire price before the customer reaches the till.
reach.learn: Which codes the till will price on its own, and which still need an override request.

evidence.claim: In equipped stores, about 54% of transactions go through self-checkout, and missed scans show up in 1% to 4.8% of transactions.
Nine in ten Dutch supermarket registers are self-service. That is a supermarket picture, not a figure for every establishment a cashier works in.
A till that holds a price file can resolve a barcode and total the bill without a separate calculator. A manual amount is the exception.
Dutch works-council consent covers tools fit to monitor staff, including per-cashier variance reports. This design does not add a scan-speed report.

assumptions: Workflow boundary: the task ends when the tabulated bill is known. Taking payment is a later cashier task and is not in these steps.

Structured contract: barcode or PLU, description, price, tax class and promotion id come from the {ERP} item file, produced by the commercial team. Admission and service PLUs are produced by the store manager on the till. Fallback: the cashier keys the amount from the shelf label and the line is flagged for a price-file fix. No model extraction.
Till calculation time is system runtime and is not cashier effort, so it is not given a share.
Self-scan is not assumed for the whole role. The 40% of scan time moved off the cashier is the equipped-store case, and the saved range uses a lower mix.
Upkeep is 8 hours per 100 cashier hours of this task, for missed-scan checks and price-file gaps. It is not zero.
National works-council rules apply if the store later reports speed or variance per cashier. This design does not.
unknowns: Whether admission and services are already on the till price file or only goods.
What share of transactions in this establishment is self-scan.
Who may override a price today, and at what amount.
How often a barcode is missing or a shelf label disagrees with the till.
research_questions: Over a typical week, what share of lines are barcode scans, PLU keys, and manual amounts?
How many price overrides does a supervisor approve per 100 transactions, and how often was the till price wrong?
What is the missed-scan rate on self-scan here, and who corrects it?

already_counted.description: Cashier checks the item name against the shelf label before keying an unmatched price.
Cashier writes the dispute reason on the override request while the customer waits.

incremental.description: Each week, clear missed self-scans and send price-file gaps back to the commercial team.
Customers scan standard baskets on a self-scan lane. This is their time, moved off the cashier, not a free gain.

approvals.approved_version: price override request snapshot with item, keyed amount, reason and shelf-label note

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Central net is about 36% of cashier time on this task after 8 hours of upkeep per 100. Low assumes a non-grocery site where almost every line stays on a staffed till and self-scan adds missed-scan checks. High assumes a mixed shop with a maintained price file, still below the centre because missed scans keep a person on the lane.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Answer incoming phone calls at the till or the desk.

steps.what: Pick up the incoming phone call at the till.
Caller states the question on the open phone call.
Answer the caller from a till note or memory.
Transfer the phone call or write a callback message.
Colleague continues the transferred incoming phone call.

tasks.design: A {TELEPHONY} greeting states the opening hours and offers a named transfer, so a call that only asks when the shop closes never reaches the till. The cashier still answers the live call. A one-page card in {DOCS} holds the stable answers, and a callback form on the phone replaces the scrap note when the call must move to a colleague. The line is not recorded.
tasks.previous_blocker: The answers lived in people's heads and on a taped note. A greeting that only said please hold did not remove the call, and the transfer list was whoever was on shift.
tasks.enabler_now: Opening hours and the transfer names are stable records. The phone system can play the hours and offer those names without a new application or a model.
tasks.still_hard: Stock, a complaint and a confused caller still need a person on the line. A wrong spoken answer is hard to take back, so the live call stays manual.
tasks.human_edge: The cashier hears urgency, a language gap or a complaint that a menu cannot place, and decides whether to answer, transfer or call back.

ambition.what: Callers who only need opening hours get them when every cashier is on the till, including the Saturday peak.

tasks.altitude: The cashier is pulled off the queue less often for a closing-time call. Live questions stay theirs. They do not gain the right to promise stock or a refund on the phone.

reach.task: Tell a caller whether a reserved item is in and when they can collect it.
reach.learn: Which phone answers the hours greeting already covers, and which must wait for a stock check.

evidence.claim: A grocery service assistant built as fixed flows plus retrieval prevented about half of contacts in one vendor case. That was a contact centre, not the till phone, so it is a ceiling for deflecting stable questions, not a plan for live calls.
Opening hours and a named transfer list are stable records a phone menu can play. The live answer at a till is still a conversation.
Tools fit to monitor staff need works-council consent where national rules say so. Scoring how each cashier handles calls would be that kind of tool. This design does not record or score calls.

assumptions: Workflow boundary: this task is answering the incoming call. Complaint handling and payment taking are other tasks.

Structured contract: the greeting uses opening hours, the pickup desk name and the transfer list. The store manager produces them. Fallback: the cashier answers from the till card, or writes a callback message. No call recording and no model.
Colleague time on a transferred call is unchanged and is not cashier time.
Upkeep is 4 hours per 100 cashier hours of this task to keep the card and the greeting current. It is not zero.
A voice bot is out of scope. A shopping chatbot would have to identify itself; this design does not use one.
unknowns: What share of calls are hours only, versus stock, complaints or a named person.
Whether the shop already has a greeting, a hunt group or a single handset at the till.
Who is allowed to promise a callback time.
research_questions: In a sample of 50 calls, how many are answered by the hours greeting alone?
How long does a live call last when the answer is on the till card, versus when it is not?
How often is a callback message lost today?

already_counted.description: Cashier still speaks the live answer, using the till card when it covers the question.
Cashier chooses the transfer name and checks the callback message before sending it.

incremental.description: Keep the hours greeting and the till card in line with this week's exceptions.
Callers listen to a short menu before a person picks up. Extra caller time, not cashier time.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Central net is about 26% of cashier time on this task after card upkeep. Low assumes most calls are live stock or complaint calls the menu cannot take. High assumes a visible share are hours-only, still under the centre because the spoken answer stays.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Answer questions on store procedures and policies.

steps.what: Listen to customers' questions on procedures or policies.
Look up the procedure or policy and quote the answering sentence.

loop.input: the customer's policy question and the short store procedure pages
loop.output: the sentence that answers it, with the page name
loop.check: The cashier reads that sentence and confirms it states the rule they will say. A matching title or page id is not enough.
loop.stop: One retrieval and one retry. If no sentence comes back, the cashier fetches the supervisor and does not guess.
loop.why_not_simpler: Keyword search returns a page. The answer is one sentence in prose, and the customer is waiting, so the cashier should not read the whole page at the till.

steps.what: Match the question to a standard procedure with no exception.
Take an exception question and the policy extract to the supervisor.
Supervisor decides whether the policy exception is allowed.
Tell the customer the standard procedure from the matched extract.
State the approved policy exception to the customer.

tasks.design: Short procedures (returns, receipts, age-restricted sales, bags) sit in {DOCS}. A bounded loop quotes the sentence that answers the question, and the cashier checks that sentence before speaking. A standard match is said at once. An exception is decided by the duty supervisor on that quoted sentence, and the cashier may state only that decision. If a screen is shown to the customer, it says the lookup is automated.
tasks.previous_blocker: Procedures sat in a binder in the back office. Search found the document, not the sentence, so the cashier read the page with the customer waiting, and evening shifts improvised when the supervisor was away.
tasks.enabler_now: The procedures are short and stable. A bounded read can quote a sentence from those pages. The cashier still checks the meaning, which is why this is not a plain search and not an agent.
tasks.still_hard: Policies that conflict, a local exception and an upset customer are not a lookup. A wrong sentence said aloud is hard to undo.
tasks.human_edge: The cashier hears that the question is not the standard one, and the supervisor decides an exception the page does not cover. The customer relationship stays with the person at the till.

ambition.what: The published returns window is said the same way on every till, including evenings when the supervisor is not on the floor.

tasks.altitude: The cashier spends less time walking to the binder. They still own what they say, and they can refuse a quote that does not support the answer. They cannot change the policy.

reach.task: Explain a hire deposit or a damage rule at the counter.
reach.learn: Which sentences are safe to read out, and which must wait for a supervisor.

evidence.claim: A grocery service assistant with about 30 fixed flows plus retrieval over FAQs prevented about half of contacts in a vendor case, and satisfaction rose 0.5 on a 5-point scale. That was a contact centre, so it bounds a till answer desk rather than describing one.
Quoting one sentence from a short procedure page is a bounded read. The cashier still has to check that the sentence is the rule they will say.
A shopping chatbot must say it is AI. A customer-facing lookup screen has to identify itself. The cashier's own speech does not become a bot.
A decision with a significant effect on a person must not be solely automated. Refusing a refund stays with the cashier and, for an exception, the supervisor.

assumptions: Workflow boundary: the task ends when the customer has been told the procedure or the approved exception. Changing the policy is not this task.

Structured contract: each procedure page has a title, a stable id, the rule text and an exception flag (standard or supervisor). The store manager produces the pages in {DOCS}. Fallback: the cashier opens the page and reads it, or fetches the supervisor. The loop does not invent a rule that is not on the page.
Logging covers the question and the page id, not a score per cashier.
Upkeep is 7 hours per 100 cashier hours of this task to fix bad quotes and update pages. It is not zero.
Supervisor time on the exception decision is other-role time and stays.
unknowns: How many procedure questions are standard versus exceptions, per 100 customers.
Whether the procedures are already in one store of documents or still in a binder and a chat thread.
Which answers the customer treats as a refusal with real effect, such as a refund.
research_questions: Which 15 questions make up most of a week's procedure talk at the till?
How often does a quoted sentence get rejected by the cashier as the wrong rule?
How often does an evening cashier invent an answer because the supervisor is not there?

already_counted.description: Cashier reads the quoted sentence and rejects it when it is not the rule they will say.
Cashier explains the exception question to the supervisor with the extract in hand.
Cashier speaks the standard procedure in their own words, staying inside the extract.

incremental.description: Fix quotes that cited the wrong sentence, and update a procedure page when the rule changes.
Supervisor reviews a sample of quotes each month. Other-role time, not cashier savings.

approvals.approved_version: policy exception decision quoting the policy extract sentence and the supervisor's yes or no

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Central net is about 38% of cashier time on this task after 7 hours of page and quote upkeep. Low assumes most questions are exceptions or upset customers, so the loop rarely fires. High assumes a short list of returns and receipt questions dominates, still under the centre because speaking the answer stays.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Page a colleague for information or assistance during a sale.

steps.what: Notice a sale needs information or assistance the till cannot give.
Send a paging request for assistance with a reason code.
Paged colleague accepts the assistance request or lets it wait.
Add the item or aisle the paging request left out.
Keep serving when nobody answers the paging request.

tasks.design: Reason buttons on the till send a staff {CHAT} or handset message with till, aisle and item, instead of a spoken public-address page. The colleague accepts on the handset. The cashier still adds a spoken detail when the reason code is not enough, and still decides to continue the sale if nobody comes. Customer-facing speakers are not used for staff calls. The voice radio stays as the fallback when the handset fails.
tasks.previous_blocker: The paging kit carried a voice code. The colleague still walked to the till to learn which item, and customers heard staff calls on the shop floor.
tasks.enabler_now: The reasons are a short fixed list: price check, carry-out, age check, spill, supervisor. A till button and a staff handset use {CHAT} or the existing radio. No new operations system and no model.
tasks.still_hard: A threat, a collapse or a customer who needs a person now is still a judgement to call at once. A noisy floor misses handsets, so the voice fallback stays, and the colleague can still be stuck with their own customer.
tasks.human_edge: The cashier judges urgency and whether to stop the sale. The colleague judges whether they can leave their own customer. A reason code does not make either call.

ambition.what: Every assistance page carries the till and the reason code, so a colleague can arrive with the answer instead of a second question.

tasks.altitude: Fewer public announcements and fewer repeated walks. The cashier does not gain the right to skip a supervisor when the reason is an override or an age check. Those still wait for the person.

reach.task: Page the storeroom for a part that is not on the counter.
reach.learn: Which requests are a reason code with an item id, and which still need a voice call.

evidence.claim: A fixed list of till, aisle and reason can travel as a staff message. Choosing to page, and coming to help, stay human judgements.

Tracking how fast each named person answers a page would be a tool fit to monitor staff and needs works-council consent where national rules require it. This design counts unanswered pages, not named speed.

assumptions: Workflow boundary: the task is the request for information or assistance. The colleague's work after they arrive, such as fetching the item, is their task.

Structured contract: reason code, till id, aisle and item code. The cashier produces the code from the sale in front of them. The store manager owns the reason list. Fallback: voice radio with the same reason spoken, when the handset does not ack. No model.
Colleague response time is other-role time and is not cashier saving. A public-address call that customers hear is removed; staff still get the message.
Upkeep is 3 hours per 100 cashier hours of this task to keep reason codes and handsets current. It is not zero.
No per-person response-time report, so the monitoring consent trigger is not pulled by this design.
unknowns: Whether the shop pages on a public address, a radio, or a shout.
How often a page goes unanswered at peak.
Which reason codes cover most calls, and which still need a voice description.
research_questions: In one busy day, how many pages are price check, carry-out, age check, spill or supervisor?
How often does the colleague arrive and still have to ask which item?
How often does the cashier continue the sale because nobody answered?

already_counted.description: Cashier still notices that this sale needs a person the till cannot replace.
Cashier adds the item or aisle when the reason code is not enough.
Cashier decides to keep serving when the page is not accepted.

incremental.description: Retune reason codes and replace a dead handset. Ongoing, not the build.
Colleagues learn the handset ack. Other-role time, not taken off the cashier.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Central net is about 39% of cashier time on this task after reason-code upkeep. Low assumes a noisy floor where the voice radio stays the normal path. High assumes most pages are a repeated reason code with an item id, still under the centre because noticing the need and giving up on a dead page stay manual.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
